headline: Left proposed changes to council rules and committee structure in committee, by 9-0 votes in each case.
summary: Councilors discussed public comment time limits and whether losing members should be able to ask for reconsideration of votes. They also talked about an annual review of council rules, a 90-day deadline for committee meetings, and a possible personnel committee. The budget review was raised as a possible move to the full council.
decisions: Kept #363, the review of the City Council's Rules and Orders, in committee, 9-0.
Kept #364, the City Council's standing committees, in committee, 9-0.

decision_evidence.quote: Holappa moved that #363, concerning a review of the City Council’s Rules and Orders, remain in committee. The motion was seconded by Varela and the motion carried 9-0.
Holappa then moved that # 364, concerning the Council’s standing committees, also remain in committee. That motion was seconded by Varela and the motion carried 9-0.

decision_titles: Review of City Council Rules and Orders (#363)
plain_text:
City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on Committee of the Whole____________________________________________ 
 met in the Council Chamber on __Monday November 9, 2026________________________ at _______6:00 PM________ 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
_________________October 27, 2026_____________________ at _________12:19 P.M.__________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
COW – Merkl (President/Chair), Davis, Prosniewski, Hapworth, King, Flynn, Smith, Sydoriak, Varela, Holappa. 
ABSENT WERE:  Turowski 
SUBJECT(S) 
#363 Meet to discuss Rules and Orders of the City Council in order to identify amendments, additions, or removals, to better 
align official and unofficial council procedures with the responsibilities of the Council.  
#364 Meet to discuss the City Council Standing Committees in order to evaluate changes to better align official and unofficial 
council procedures with the responsibilities of the Council. 
Discussion on #363 Rules & Orders of the City Council 
Holappa thanked those attending the meeting, both in person and online, and explained that the purpose of raising potential 
changes to the Council’s Rules and Orders was to encourage discussion among members, identify areas for improvement, and 
make Council proceedings more efficient and effective in serving constituents. The first issue involved reconsideration rules 
under Sections 14 and 15. She suggested either revising those provisions to align with Robert’s Rules of Order or removing 
them and deferring to Robert’s Rules, which generally requires a member seeking reconsideration to have voted on the 
prevailing side. She argued that Salem’s current rule, which allows any member to request reconsideration after a vote, could 
be used to obstruct or delay Council business. As an example, Holappa cited a recent order concerning temporary police 
cameras, which had broad Council support but could have been delayed by at least two weeks if a member who voted against 
it had requested reconsideration. 
The second issue concerned public comment under Section 26(C)(1). Holappa proposed establishing a minimum public 
comment period of 90 seconds, noting that speakers often do not know how much time they will be given when preparing 
their remarks and that being cut short can be frustrating. Although the rules allow the Council president to extend public 
comment or the Council to approve an extension by majority vote, Holappa expressed concern that discretionary extensions 
could create perceptions of favoritism or unequal treatment depending on the topic. A guaranteed 90-second minimum, she 
argued, would provide residents with a reasonable opportunity to express their views while maintaining an orderly meeting. 
Merkl confirmed that City Solicitor James Wellock had verified that, under Robert’s Rules of Order, only a member who voted 
with the prevailing side may move for reconsideration, although Salem’s current rules differ and anyone can make a motion.
Varela supported the proposed reconsideration rule change, suggesting Salem’s existing language may have been carried over 
from an earlier procedural manual and was not updated when the Council began implementing Robert’s Rules of Order a few 
years ago. 
King supported aligning Salem’s reconsideration rules with Robert’s Rules of Order, arguing that consistency would make 
Council procedures easier for new members and the public to understand unless there is a compelling reason to deviate. 
Sydoriak leaned toward adopting Robert’s Rules of Order but suggested a possible compromise that would limit 
reconsideration by the losing side for certain time-sensitive matters, such as the budget and zoning ordinances, while allowing 
it for other types of motions or orders. 
Hapworth acknowledged the competing priorities of government efficiency and protecting minority voices, noting that 
allowing the losing side to request reconsideration could give members an opportunity to correct mistakes or change their 
votes after further reflection; however, Hapworth also recognized the potential for delays on time-sensitive matters, such as 
the budget, and was not opposed to eliminating the current rule. 
Smith supported retaining the current reconsideration rule, arguing that it gives minority members an opportunity to raise 
additional arguments and persuade colleagues after a vote; Smith noted that time-sensitive matters can be expedited by using 
a motion to reconsider that does not prevail, thereby ending further reconsideration attempts and allowing the item to 
proceed. 
Davis supported aligning Salem’s reconsideration rules with Robert’s Rules of Order, arguing that minority members already 
have opportunities to express their views through their votes and comments during debate and that allowing losing members 
to request another vote generally serves little purpose when the outcome is unlikely to change. 
Varela supported establishing a 90-second minimum for public comment, arguing that Council has a responsibility to listen to 
residents regardless of attendance and that providing a guaranteed speaking time respects those who prepare remarks for the 
meeting. 
King supported a 90-second minimum for public comment and suggested extending the requirement to committee meetings 
as well as regular Council meetings to ensure residents receive the same guaranteed speaking time at all public meetings. 
Hapworth expressed some reservations about establishing a mandatory 90-second minimum for public comment, warning that 
a fixed requirement could create delays during time-sensitive matters, particularly zoning proceedings with statutory 
deadlines, and potentially allow opponents to prolong meetings. Hapworth also noted that giving the Council president 
discretion to extend speaking time could raise concerns about unequal treatment but questioned whether a formal minimum 
was necessary given that instances of speakers receiving less than a minute had been limited. 
Prosniewski supported establishing a 90-second public comment period, arguing that 30 seconds is insufficient for speakers to 
introduce themselves and adequately express their views. Prosniewski also emphasized the need for a maximum speaking time 
to prevent intentional filibustering but maintained that 90 seconds provides a reasonable opportunity for residents to be heard 
and that listening to public comment is part of the Council’s responsibility. 
Sydoriak suggested that if the Council is concerned about filibustering, it should also consider limiting the number of people 
permitted to speak, arguing that the number of speakers, rather than the time allotted to each individual, could be the greater 
source of delays. Sydoriak clarified that this was offered as another consideration, not a formal proposal. 
King explained that the proposed 90-second minimum would retain the existing 15-minute cap on public comment, while 
allowing the Council President or a majority vote of the Council to extend the overall time. For example, if 15 people signed up, 
the Council could extend the period to accommodate 90 seconds per speaker; if 100 people signed up, it could establish a 
longer overall limit while guaranteeing each speaker at least 90 seconds and allowing those who finish early to yield time to 
others. King suggested applying the change only to regular Council meetings, where speakers sign up in advance, rather than 
committee meetings, which present different logistical challenges.
Smith asked for clarification on how the proposed 90-second minimum would work alongside the existing 15-minute public 
comment limit. Smith questioned whether the available time would be distributed among speakers when only a few people 
sign up, allowing longer remarks, or whether every speaker would receive 90 seconds regardless of attendance. 
King clarified that the current practice is generally to allow up to three minutes per speaker at regular meetings, rather than 
automatically dividing the 15-minute public comment limit among those who sign up. King supported establishing a 
guaranteed 90-second minimum so residents can prepare remarks and know what to expect, while allowing the Council to 
reduce speaking time by majority vote when an unusually large number of people sign up. King noted that lengthy public 
comment periods can disrupt meetings, particularly when many speakers attend hearings, but argued that a predictable 
minimum would provide a fairer process. 
Merkl explained that she had previously consulted with the City Solicitor about the issue, noting the difficulty of guaranteeing 
speaking time while preventing meetings from being extended excessively or creating inconsistent treatment between 
meetings. She recommended that Councilors consult the solicitor about the legal and procedural implications, emphasizing the 
need for clear safeguards that preserve both an equitable public comment process and the Council’s ability to keep meetings 
on track. Merkl also clarified that the discussion concerned regular Council meetings, not hearings or committee meetings. 
Hapworth cautioned against giving the full Council authority to extend or reduce public comment time by majority vote, 
arguing that decisions about recognizing speakers and managing public comment should remain with the presiding chair. 
Hapworth also emphasized the public’s interest in following the full Council agenda, including other city business, and warned 
that lengthy public comment periods could be used to delay meetings and prevent residents from accessing information about 
other matters. Hapworth maintained that the existing 15-minute overall limit and general practice of allowing up to three 
minutes per speaker had worked reasonably well, with very few instances in which speakers received less than a minute. 
Holappa acknowledged the different concerns raised during the discussion and suggested establishing a clear overall time limit 
for public comment. Holappa questioned whether the existing 15-minute cap was sufficient or should be extended, proposing 
that speakers be heard in sign-up order for a guaranteed minimum amount of time until the overall limit is reached, even if 
that meant a substantially longer public comment period. 
Varela argued that the existing rules already give the chair or a majority of the Council discretion to extend public comment 
when needed. Varela said that even if 15 speakers each received 90 seconds, the public comment period would last only about 
25 to 30 minutes and maintained that the chair and Council would retain control over the overall time, preventing speakers 
from using the process to deliberately delay meetings. Varela also expressed support for encouraging greater public 
participation. 
Davis expressed concern that establishing a 90-second minimum without addressing the existing 15-minute overall limit could 
result in some residents being allowed to speak while others who signed up are excluded. Davis suggested setting the 
minimum at 60 seconds instead, arguing that this would avoid extremely short speaking times while helping ensure that 
everyone who signs up has an opportunity to address the Council. Davis added that even if 100 people signed up, the public 
comment period would last approximately one hour. 
Prosniewski emphasized the need for a clear, concise preamble explaining the public comment rules, potentially drafted with 
input from the City Solicitor. Prosniewski supported guaranteeing speakers at least 90 seconds while retaining a three-minute 
maximum, arguing that this provides sufficient time to express their views. Prosniewski also stressed that public comment is 
not a debate or question-and-answer period and that the rules should clearly explain the time limits and expectations to 
residents. 
Smith strongly supported establishing a guaranteed minimum speaking time, whether 60 or 90 seconds, so residents know 
what to expect before attending a meeting and are encouraged to participate. Smith argued that high public attendance 
should be viewed as a positive sign of civic engagement rather than simply a potential disruption, noting that previous large 
public hearings had provided valuable insight into residents’ views. Smith also pointed out that advance sign-ups give the 
Council notice of expected participation and an opportunity to address unusually large numbers of speakers and suggested 
consulting the City Solicitor before moving forward. 
Other rules discussion –
King proposed adding an annual Rules and Orders meeting to the Council’s procedures, as many other Massachusetts 
communities do. Under this approach, the Council would continue operating under the previous year’s rules until it holds a 
scheduled meeting, typically before its first regular meeting of the year, to review and vote on updated rules. King argued that 
making this discussion a routine annual process would reduce tension surrounding special meetings called to address specific 
rule changes and ensure the Council regularly has an opportunity to review its procedures, even in years when no changes are 
needed. King had not yet consulted the City Solicitor about the appropriate language for the proposal. 
Hapworth supported King’s proposal for an annual Rules and Orders review, noting that some outdated provisions remain in 
place simply because no one has revisited them. Hapworth said a regularly scheduled annual meeting would ensure the 
Council reviews its rules at each new term, rather than relying on someone to initiate a separate meeting and bring forward 
specific changes. As an example, Hapworth recalled that the Council had continued requiring physical mailing of meeting 
notices until around 2023 or 2024 because the rule had not been reviewed. 
Holappa expressed strong support for King’s proposal for an annual Rules and Orders meeting, particularly the suggested 
timing at the beginning of each Council session. Holappa said the meeting would provide an opportunity to review procedures 
and help newly elected or incoming Council members better understand the Council’s rules and how it conducts its business. 
Varela supported holding an annual Rules and Orders meeting at the beginning of each year, arguing that it would establish a 
consistent best practice and ensure new councillors understand that Council rules can be reviewed and changed. Varela said 
the meeting would promote transparency, prevent more experienced councillors from taking advantage of newer members’ 
unfamiliarity with the process, and ensure everyone begins the year with a shared understanding of the rules and the ability to 
propose changes. 
Merkl offered a minor housekeeping example for the annual Rules and Orders review, pointing to inconsistent wording in the 
current rules regarding whether Council members should “rise and stand” or “stand adjourned.” She said this illustrated the 
value of periodically reviewing the rules for basic corrections and cleanup before concluding discussion of King’s proposal. 
Hapworth identified a clerical error in Section 29B on page 21 of the Rules and Orders, which incorrectly references Section 32 
in connection with finance matters. Hapworth said the reference should be changed to Section 30, suggesting the error 
resulted from a previous addition to the rules that was not accompanied by an update to the cross-reference. 
Davis suggested adding a rule establishing a reasonable deadline for committees to hold meetings after an item is referred to 
them by Council. Davis noted that some communities, including Boston, require committee consideration within 30 calendar 
days, although Davis felt that timeframe might be too short. Davis proposed allowing extensions for legitimate reasons, such as 
additional research or legal review, and said the goal would be to ensure that items approved for committee referral are 
addressed within a reasonable period. 
Sydoriak noted discrepancies between the printed Rules and Orders and the versions available online and in the municipal 
code, recommending that all versions be reconciled before Council decides which document to amend. As an example, the 
printed copy incorrectly referenced Section 32 in Section 29B, while the online version correctly cited Section 30. 
Hapworth stated regarding Davis’s suggestion to establish deadlines for committee consideration, he cautioned against 
imposing an arbitrary timeframe, arguing that current informal practices had generally worked and that items sometimes 
remain in committee for strategic or practical reasons before being brought forward. He acknowledged that a committee chair 
could potentially delay an item but noted that Council may have the ability to vote to remove an item from committee and 
bring it before the full Council.  
Merkl said she would confirm the procedure and provide the committee with clarification.  
Varela supported establishing a deadline, suggesting 90 days rather than 30, and argued that a reasonable timeframe would 
help prevent committee chairs from indefinitely delaying issues that deserve public discussion. 
King supported requiring items referred to committee to receive an initial committee meeting within 90 days, agreeing that 
the proposed 30-day deadline was too short. King said a 90-day requirement would establish a reasonable expectation that 
newly introduced legislation receives an initial hearing. However, King cautioned against requiring another meeting every 90
days for items that remain in committee, noting that some proposals may need additional time for research, consultation with 
experts, or coordination with city departments before they are ready for further consideration. Repeated deadlines could force 
Council to revisit proposals that are not yet ready or that have limited support. King therefore suggested requiring an initial 
meeting within 90 days, while leaving subsequent meetings during the same calendar year to the committee chair’s discretion 
as a compromise that would ensure timely initial consideration without creating unintended consequences. 
Davis clarified that the 30-day rule in Boston applies to an item’s initial committee meeting, rather than requiring repeated 
meetings or a vote within that timeframe. Davis supported establishing a deadline for initial consideration and noted that the 
ability of Council to pull an item out of committee does not address the same concern, since members may want a committee 
discussion before voting. Davis suggested exploring a mechanism that would allow councillors, through action at a Council 
meeting, to require an item to be scheduled for its initial committee discussion, and recommended consulting the City Solicitor 
about what procedures would be permissible. 
Holappa supported establishing a 90-day deadline for an item’s initial committee meeting, describing it as a reasonable 
timeframe. Holappa added that pairing the requirement with regular Rules and Orders review meetings would allow future 
Councils to assess whether the policy is working, explain any concerns, and amend the rules as needed. 
Sydoriak agreed with King that any 90-day requirement should apply only to an item’s initial committee meeting, with 
subsequent meetings left explicitly to the committee chair’s discretion. Sydoriak noted that committees such as the 
Ordinances, Licenses and Legal Affairs (OLLA) Committee often have heavy workloads, requiring the chair to prioritize new 
items and determine which matters need attention before others already awaiting discussion. 
Hapworth viewed a 90-day deadline for an initial committee meeting as a way to formalize an existing best practice, saying the 
timeframe seemed reasonable and that most committee chairs already bring items forward within that period. Hapworth 
cautioned, however, that codifying the requirement could create unintended complications, particularly when proposals need 
additional information or are not yet ready for discussion. Hapworth supported applying the deadline only to the initial 
meeting, emphasizing that items may appropriately remain in committee for six months or longer while Council members 
gather information, reconsider their positions, or determine when a proposal is ready to move forward. 
Public Comment  
Jeff Cohen of 12 Hancock Street emphasized the importance of public participation and opposed limiting the number of people 
allowed to speak at Council meetings. He recalled that Salem previously had no 15-minute public comment limit and cited the 
2017 sanctuary city ordinance meeting, which drew more than 800 people and continued until 2 a.m. Based on his experiences 
speaking before other municipal councils, Cohen suggested guaranteeing each speaker 90 seconds, rather than maintaining a 
15-minute overall limit, and installing a visible countdown clock to help speakers manage their time and ensure they are not 
cut off unexpectedly. He also urged Council to encourage broader public participation and allow residents to express their 
views without interruption, citing the Southborough court case and his understanding that meeting chairs cannot require 
civility during public testimony. Cohen concluded that a visible timer would help make public comment more predictable and 
ensure speakers know how much time they have. 
Steve Kapantis opposed changing the reconsideration rules to limit motions to members who voted with the prevailing side, 
arguing that any resulting delay would generally be no longer than two weeks and that the existing rule protects minority 
members, particularly on close votes. He also challenged Council’s emphasis on revising its rules, arguing that councillors 
should first receive training on Robert’s Rules, the City Council’s own procedures, and the Open Meeting Law, and consistently 
follow the rules already in place. Kapantis cited examples of councillors speaking more than twice on an issue and inconsistent 
enforcement of restrictions on applause, arguing that Council should focus on understanding and applying its own rules before 
changing those governing public participation. 
Discussion on # 364 City Council Standing Committees  
Holappa explained that the proposed orders were intentionally presented separately to identify issues and opportunities for 
discussion without prescribing specific solutions. Regarding the committee discussion, she encouraged members to remain 
open to considering different approaches, noting that an issue initially raised for committee consideration might ultimately be 
better addressed through a change to Council rules.
Varela called for a broader review of Salem’s committee structure, arguing that too much responsibility falls on the OLLA 
Committee and that other existing committees could be used more effectively to distribute workloads and provide more 
opportunities for discussion. He suggested considering whether OLLA’s responsibilities should be divided among other 
committees and said the Council should examine how other communities organize their committees. Varela also proposed 
creating a personnel committee to provide more thorough review of appointments and reappointments to city boards and 
commissions. Citing practices in Lynn and Woburn, he described how personnel committees can review appointments and 
conduct interviews rather than routinely approving nominees without substantial discussion. Varela said Salem should make 
more thoughtful use of its authority to vet board and commission appointments, while recognizing that changing the mayor’s 
authority over department heads would require a charter change and was not the immediate proposal. 
King expressed strong support for the concept of a personnel committee, citing similar practices in Marlborough and arguing 
that a more substantive appointment process would help attract and recognize qualified people serving on city boards and 
commissions. King criticized the tendency to approve appointments as a formality and said nominees deserve a more 
thoughtful review. King also cautioned that Council should carefully consider committee size and structure, suggesting five 
members as a preferable number to avoid potential quorum complications associated with smaller committees. 
Holappa supported creating a personnel committee and argued that the Council should consistently interview or speak with all 
nominees for boards and commissions, as well as department head appointments and reappointments, rather than singling 
out individuals for scrutiny only when a councillor requests a discussion. Citing Marlborough’s use of subcommittees and 
Salem’s larger number of boards and commissions (47 compared with Marlborough’s 20), Holappa said Salem has an even 
greater need for a formal review process. She also supported reconsidering the structure of the Ordinances, Licenses, and 
Legal Affairs Committee, questioning why such varied matters are grouped together. She favored topic-focused 
subcommittees for ordinance and legislative work, similar to the public health, safety, and environment committee, arguing 
that this approach would allow the Council President to assign members based on their expertise and interests and give 
councillors more meaningful choices in their committee work. 
Smith supported reviewing the Council’s committee structure and suggested that some of the workload assigned to OLLA 
could instead be directed to existing committees with more appropriate responsibilities. He noted that Public Health, Safety, 
and the Environment could handle matters involving public health, safety, and environment concerns; Government Services 
could address municipal department operations; and Community and Economic Development could take on housing, business, 
and related issues. He suggested creating one or two additional specialized committees, rather than substantially expanding 
the committee system, so matters could receive more focused attention from councillors with relevant knowledge and 
interests. He said specialization would reduce individual workloads and allow councillors to develop greater familiarity with the 
issues and regulations within their assigned areas. Smith also supported establishing a personnel committee, although he 
acknowledged that reviewing department head appointments may raise different concerns from reviewing boards and 
commissions. Given Salem’s 47 boards and commissions, he said a more formal appointment process could encourage greater 
consideration and seriousness among appointees. 
Hapworth supported distributing the Council’s workload more evenly among committees, noting that Salem’s Plan B 
government structure was designed to allow committees to develop expertise in specific areas rather than expecting every 
councillor to understand every issue. The councillor said OLLA has become a catch-all, partly because of councillor turnover 
and a shortage of experienced committee chairs. With experienced leadership, however, matters could be referred to the 
committees best suited to handle them without changing the existing rules or committee structure. He cited the camping 
ordinance, which was handled entirely by the Public Health, Safety, and Environment Committee, as an example of how this 
approach can work.  Regarding a proposed personnel committee, Hapworth was open to reviewing appointments to boards 
and commissions but urged caution about requiring volunteers to appear before a committee for public interviews, describing 
the process as potentially uncomfortable and burdensome. He noted that councillors can often contact nominees directly to 
learn more about them. However, Hapworth strongly opposed requiring department heads to appear before the Council for 
interviews, arguing that the mayor has operational authority over those positions and that putting city employees through a 
public process to seek or retain their jobs would exceed the Council’s appropriate oversight role.  
Sydoriak said the Council needs to clarify what its oversight responsibility means when voting on appointments, questioning 
the purpose of its approval authority if the process amounts to little more than a rubber stamp. While acknowledging concerns 
about putting people’s jobs and livelihoods at risk, he said the Council should better define the limits and purpose of its role. 
He supported creating a personnel committee to establish a more consistent framework and encourage councillors to prepare
for appointment reviews. If interviews are conducted, he emphasized that all candidates should be asked consistent questions 
and treated equally, as with the Community Preservation Committee appointment process. Sydoriak also supported 
distributing ordinance and legislative work among committees but suggested first developing a stronger practice of discussing 
where matters should be referred rather than creating rigid categories. He cautioned that some issues may fit multiple 
committees or fall outside established areas, so councillors should work together to identify the most appropriate committee 
before formalizing structural changes. 
Merkl pointed to the Council’s committee descriptions in the meeting materials, noting that they allow more flexibility in 
assigning matters than current practices may suggest. She cited Government Services as an underutilized committee that could 
potentially review appointments, given its responsibility for matters involving the adequacy of services provided by municipal 
departments. Rather than automatically sending matters to Ordinances, Licenses, and Legal Affairs simply because they involve 
ordinances, Merkl encouraged greater use of other committees based on their stated responsibilities. 
Varela described the discussion as an initial effort to distribute the Council’s workload more evenly so that Ordinances, 
Licenses, and Legal Affairs does not handle such a large share of the work. He suggested that matters such as drain layer 
bonds, licenses, and claims could be assigned to Government Services, allowing OLLA to focus on more substantive matters. If 
another committee is created, he recommended revising the descriptions and responsibilities of existing committees, 
particularly Government Services and Community and Economic Development, to make better use of them. He said the goal is 
to improve the productivity of meetings and discussions and help the Council accomplish more by being thoughtful about 
where matters are referred. 
Merkl recommended consulting the City Solicitor before changing which committees handle licensing matters or other 
responsibilities, to ensure any proposed changes comply with Massachusetts General Law and do not conflict with required 
legal procedures. 
Hapworth questioned whether the annual budget review should remain with the Administration and Finance Committee or be 
referred to the Committee of the Whole so all councillors could participate throughout the process, rather than weighing in 
only when the budget reaches the full Council for approval. He argued that the budget is one of the Council’s most important 
responsibilities and that involving the entire body could provide members with greater input and shared responsibility. 
Although he initially questioned whether a larger committee would make achieving a quorum more difficult, he suggested that 
having more members available could actually make scheduling meetings easier. 
Varela supported exploring the proposal, saying the entire Council should have a voice in the budget process because of its 
importance. He acknowledged that maintaining a quorum could be challenging but felt broader participation would give 
councillors more ownership of budget discussions. 
Smith opposed moving the budget to the Committee of the Whole, arguing that the Administration and Finance Committee 
provides the specialization and focused analysis needed for the process. He pointed out that the City’s ordinances authorize 
the Council to hire a budget analyst to review the budget on its behalf, although he was unsure when that provision was last 
used. He suggested exploring that resource to strengthen the committee’s expertise and said the full Council already has an 
opportunity to raise concerns and make changes when the budget comes forward for approval. 
Davis said he hadn’t thought about moving the budget to the Committee of the Whole but found it compelling after hearing 
Hapworth’s reasoning. He questioned why the entire Council would not participate in a responsibility as central to its work as 
the annual budget, particularly because the process occurs every year and involves an extended series of meetings rather than 
a one-time issue.  Davis added that, if the budget process were moved to the Committee of the Whole, the Council President 
could appoint another councillor to chair those meetings. Given the significant time and responsibility involved in overseeing 
the budget, Davis said the President should not necessarily have to manage those meetings in addition to the other duties of 
the office. 
Public Comment  
Jeff Cohen of 12 Hancock Street criticized the budget discussion, saying that, based on his experience as a former councillor 
and nearly 18 years of attending budget meetings, the Council has limited ability to change the proposed budget and rarely 
makes more than a few adjustments. He argued that the budget ultimately comes before the full Council for consideration and
questioned the need to change the existing process. He also opposed expanding the number of committees, saying councillors 
could address OLLA’s workload by referring matters to more appropriate existing committees. 
Cohen focused on the City’s 47 boards and commissions, drawing on his experience serving as chair of two boards for several 
years. He emphasized that recruiting and retaining volunteers is difficult, particularly for boards such as Planning and 
Conservation, which require substantial preparation and time commitments, often without compensation. He expressed 
gratitude for residents willing to serve and cautioned against making the appointment process more burdensome by requiring 
volunteers to appear before a committee and explain why they deserve a position. He noted that applicants already submit a 
letter and résumé to the mayor and commit significant time to public service. Rather than adding interviews, he suggested the 
Council focus on better communication with appointees, recalling that he had previously tried to contact every newly 
appointed board member and that access to their contact information had not always been readily available. 
Holappa moved that #363, concerning a review of the City Council’s Rules and Orders, remain in committee. The motion was 
seconded by Varela and the motion carried 9-0. Holappa then moved that # 364, concerning the Council’s standing 
committees, also remain in committee. That motion was seconded by Varela and the motion carried 9-0.  
Note: Councillor King left prior to the above votes. 
On the motion of C. Holappa the meeting adjourned at 7:47 P.M. 
 
       Alice Merkl                                       MBC 
        (Chairperson)
